# knowmoretabs — slices

> Every tab you ever had open, kept and searchable.

## What people want, and which slice delivers it

| Capability | Want | Delivered by |
|---|---|---|
| `save-now` | Save what's open right now, in one command | 1 `capture` |
| `never-lose` | Never lose a snapshot to a crash or a half-written file | 1 `capture` |
| `survive-updates` | Keep working when my browser changes its format | 1 `capture` |
| `offline-forever` | Read my archive offline, years from now | 2 `library` |
| `find-old-page` | Find a page I had open months ago | 2 `library` |
| `when-and-where` | See when and where a page was open | 2 `library` |
| `forget-pages` | Forget pages I don't want to see again | 3 `triage` |
| `triage-in-bulk` | Clear a backlog without touching the terminal | 3 `triage` |
| `my-browser` | Use the browser I actually use | 4 `browsers` |
| `my-platform` | Use it on my Linux box or my work Windows machine | 5 `platforms` |
| `easy-install` | Install it without installing a toolchain first | 6 `release` |

## Build order

### 1. Capture a snapshot (`capture`) — done

- Delivers: save-now, never-lose, survive-updates
- Depends on: —

**Ships.** `knowmoretabs save` finds the newest Chrome session on macOS, parses it, and
writes an immutable dated snapshot: the tabs as JSON plus a verbatim copy of
the session file. Tab groups — name, colour, membership — and each tab's
last-active time are parsed here because the data model is the thing hardest
to change later, even though nothing displays them until slice 2. A session
matching the previous snapshot is skipped. An interrupted run leaves the
archive exactly as it was. If Chrome's encrypted session files are newer than
its cleartext ones, the run refuses rather than saving stale tabs as current.

**Intent.** The tracer bullet. Everything downstream reads what this writes, so its data
model and its durability guarantees are the two decisions hardest to change
later. The project's foundation — workspace, lints, CI, the slice lint itself —
rides along here rather than becoming a horizontal slice of its own.

### 2. The offline library (`library`) — done

- Delivers: offline-forever, find-old-page, when-and-where
- Depends on: capture

**Ships.** `knowmoretabs export` writes a static site: every page you have ever had open,
listed once, with search, filters and a per-page history of the snapshots and
windows it appeared in. `knowmoretabs list` shows the same from the terminal.
Opens from `file://` with no server and no network.

**Intent.** This is where a pile of snapshots becomes a thing worth having. The frontend
built here is the same frontend slice 3 serves, so it is written to work
against either an embedded JSON blob or a fetch — one renderer, two hosts.

### 3. Serve and triage (`triage`) — done

- Delivers: forget-pages, triage-in-bulk
- Depends on: library

**Ships.** `knowmoretabs serve` runs the library on 127.0.0.1 with the same assets and a
small JSON API. Forget and restore become real buttons with bulk selection and
undo. The `forget` and `restore` CLI commands do the same thing headlessly.
Snapshots are never touched: forgetting hides a page, it does not delete it.

**Intent.** The reason the project stopped being a script. Every feature asked for so far
points at a button on the page, and a button needs somewhere to POST to.

### 4. The browser you actually use (`browsers`) — done

- Delivers: my-browser
- Depends on: capture

**Ships.** Brave, Edge, Chromium and Vivaldi alongside Chrome, with profile discovery and
`--browser` / `--profile`, and a sensible answer when three browsers are
installed.

**Intent.** Pure reach. It is slice 4 rather than slice 1 because a second browser teaches
you nothing the first one did not, and it is cheap once the browser table is
the only thing that varies.

### 5. Linux and Windows (`platforms`) — done

- Delivers: my-platform
- Depends on: browsers

**Ships.** Session discovery on Linux and Windows, path handling that survives both, and
a CI matrix that proves it rather than assuming it.

**Intent.** Deferred this far because every platform doubles the CI bill and none of it is
testable without a real profile on a real machine. Doing it after the browser
table exists means one table gains a column, not three code paths.

### 6. Install it in one line (`release`) — planned

- Delivers: easy-install
- Depends on: platforms

**Ships.** Tagged releases with prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux and Windows, a
changelog, install instructions that do not begin with "first install Rust",
and a crate ready to publish.

**Intent.** A personal tool published openly still has to be installable by someone who
does not care what it is written in. Publishing to a registry is a separate,
explicit decision — this slice builds the machinery and leaves the trigger
unpulled.

## Prepared for, deliberately not built

### `live-tabs` — See my live tabs exactly, not the last session written to disk

- Prepared by: capture, browsers

Needs a browser extension, and it is the most direct route to what the product
is for: an extension sees the tabs on screen at that moment, on every Chromium
browser, before and after Chrome encrypts session storage. A session file lags
the screen by a flush, and is what can be read after a crash or with the
browser closed. Cost: a "Read your browsing history" prompt, a Web Store
listing with its fee and review queue, an install step per browser and
platform, and inverted control: stable Chrome lets no process pull tabs, so
the browser pushes on its own schedule and `save` from cron never sees live
tabs. The capture layer keeps its source abstract, so adding one is additive.
Design: docs/research/native-messaging.md.

### `arc` — Use it with Arc

- Prepared by: browsers

Arc is Chromium-based and writes SNSS files, but only `Tabs_*` — its open-tab
model lives in `StorableSidebar.json`, a proprietary schema of Spaces and a
pinned sidebar. Parsing its session files would snapshot the wrong thing
convincingly, which is worse than not supporting it. Arc needs a second source
adapter, not a row in the browser table.

### `notes-tags` — Tag a page and write myself a note about it

- Prepared by: triage

`library.json` already carries per-URL user state; forgetting is the first and
most-wanted instance of it. Tags earn their place once triage is in daily use
and the shape of what people want to record is known, rather than guessed.

### `fulltext` — Search what was on the page, not just its title

- Prepared by: —

Means fetching and storing page bodies: network traffic, a much larger archive,
and a privacy story that changes completely. Titles and URLs answer most
searches. This is a different product until proven otherwise.

### `scale-index` — Stay instant with years of snapshots

- Prepared by: library, triage

Fifty snapshots of three hundred tabs is fifteen thousand rows; reading JSON
into memory is instant and costs no dependency, no migration and no corruption
mode. A rebuildable SQLite index is the answer when a measured query is slow,
and the JSON snapshots stay the source of truth when it arrives.

### `close-live-tabs` — Close the tabs I have triaged, in the browser

- Prepared by: —

Requires driving the live browser, and makes a read-only tool capable of
destroying the thing it archives. If it is ever built it is opt-in, explicit,
and only after a snapshot has been taken.

### `encrypted-archive` — Keep the archive encrypted at rest

- Prepared by: capture

The archive is a record of everything you browse. Today it is protected by
0700 and by never leaving the machine. Encryption means key management, which
means a way to lock yourself out of your own history. Worth doing properly or
not at all.
